messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 69
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Fast Food Worker
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 76

She still wears her uniform home from the fast food restaurant, the smell of fryer oil clinging to her cardigan. Most nights she sits in the living room with the lights off, the television muted, listening. Her husband, Amir, calls to her from the kitchen—*the rice is getting cold*—but she cannot move. The sound of footsteps on the sidewalk outside sends a current through her chest. She waits for the shadow to pass.

It started three years ago, when she was sixty-six. A customer, early thirties, came to the drive-through window every Tuesday evening. He always ordered the same thing: a junior chicken, no pickles, a large Diet Coke. She remembers his voice—soft, almost gentle. He began to linger. He would ask how her day was, comment on her smile, call her *habibti*. At first she felt flattered. Then he started coming every day. He memorized her shift. He told her she was beautiful, that she deserved a real man, not an old one who didn’t appreciate her.

She mentioned it to her manager, who told her to smile and be polite. She didn’t tell Amir—she was embarrassed, ashamed, afraid he would say she had encouraged it. The man began leaving notes on her car windshield. *I know where you live. I saw you buying bread.* She started taking different routes home, checking the rearview mirror until her neck ached.

The police were called when he followed her into the restaurant, past the counter, and stood three feet from her register, staring. The officers told her he hadn’t broken the law, not yet. They gave her a paper with a case number. She pinned it to the refrigerator, where it yellowed, unread.

Now she cannot stand at the register without scanning the parking lot. A customer who leans forward, who speaks too quietly, who lingers after paying—she feels her throat close. She has stopped taking her break outside. She eats alone in the freezer, shivering, because there are no windows. Her hands shake when she hands over change. The other workers think she is old and slow. They do not know that she counts the steps from the counter to the back door, that she has rehearsed what she would scream.

She avoids the neighborhood grocery. She will not answer the door after dark. She wakes at three in the morning certain she hears a key in the lock. Her heart pounds so hard she feels it in her teeth. Amir tried to hold her once, and she pushed him away, crying, unable to explain that the touch felt like a threat.

She has not worn her favorite scarf in a year. It is red. He once said it reminded him of blood. She threw it in the trash, then fished it out, then stuffed it deep in a drawer.

At work she is always tired, always on edge. The smell of oil used to mean nothing. Now it reminds her of the Tuesday evenings, the way the headlights of his car would linger in the drive-through lane, the way his head tilted as he watched her walk to her car.

She does not tell anyone about the nightmares. In them, he is always standing in her kitchen. Sometimes he is holding the Diet Coke. Sometimes he is holding nothing. He never speaks. She wakes up with her jaw clamped shut, the roof of her mouth dry.

Amir asks why she looks so frightened all the time. She tells him she is just getting old. She knows he does not believe her. But the word *stalking* feels too heavy to say out loud, as if saying it would make it permanent, as if she would have to admit that the fear never really went away. It only learned to live inside her chest, small and patient, waiting for the next Tuesday.
